newsitem.title: FRANCE: Meeting on Bosnia to back peace consolidation plan.
newsitem.headline: Meeting on Bosnia to back peace consolidation plan.

text.p: Bosnia's three co-presidents met major powers on Thursday to approve a two-year plan intended to stabilise fragile peace in the former Yugoslav republic.

Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders elected in September were to pledge actions to complete joint institutions, enable return of some two million refugees, ensure freedom of movement and press freedom and build a market economy over two years.
In return, the international community will commit itself at the one-day conference to continue assistance in rebuilding Bosnia's administration and economy after nearly four years of bitter war.

"We had some good progress but a lot of work remains to be done to reunite the country," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on arrival at the Kleber conference centre near the Arc de Triomphe.

However, a widely-expected decision to keep an international military presence in Bosnia when the mandate of the NATO-led Peace Implementation Force (IFOR) expires at the end of the year will be taken after further deliberation at NATO headquarters in Brussels, and not discussed in Paris, officials said.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher met the Bosnian co-presidents on the eve of the conference and said the implementation of the Dayton peace agreement, signed a year ago, was at a "very critical stage" after a clash on Tuesday in which two Moslem refugees were killed.
"I urge all the people in Bosnia to avoid the kind of incident that took place (on Tuesday). That is not constructive and can only harm efforts to advance peace there," he said.
Christopher pressed Moslem Alija Izetbegovic, Serb Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat Kresimir Zubak to implement fully the Dayton peace accord signed a year ago.
He singled out the return of refugees, the holding of municipal elections and building a more active international police force as key issues.
A senior U.S. official held late night talks with the three leaders to try to help them thrash out a joint cabinet list.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, co-chairing the conference with international mediator Carl Bildt, told reporters the aim was to lay the foundations of a "moral contract" between the international community and Bosnia.
He said the rival factions must also cooperate more fully with the international tribunal in the Hague in bringing wanted war criminals to justice. Only a handful have been handed over so far.

A French draft of the proposed declaration obtained by Reuters calls for Bosnia to pledge to have a working cabinet, parliament, central bank, constitutional court and military committee by next March at the latest.
Bosnian officials said little progress was made overnight in Paris in discussions on a cabinet.

A second conference in London in December will adopt a more detailed action programme for the next year, by which time NATO is likely to have formally approved a slimmed-down peacekeeping force to succeed IFOR.
"The main decisions are to be taken in London," Rifkind told reporters. "But this is a very important occasion to draw attention to the outstanding problems."

Thursday's conference will be relatively brief, with a three-hour working session to approve the statement of guiding principles, a lunch and a final ceremony at President Jacques Chirac's Elysee palace.

Countries attending were Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and rump Yugoslavia, the United States, Russia, France, Britain, Germany, Italy, Canada, the Netherlands, Ireland as current president of the European Union and Turkey, representing the Islamic Conference Organisation.
Several international organisations were also represented: the United Nations, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe and NATO.
